Active particle systems model animals as self-propelled particles with effective interactions.
Nonreciprocal forces between animals violate Newton's third law and arise naturally in contests.
The contest model treats contestants as active Brownian particles governed by an overdamped Langevin equation.
Effective potentials include a resource potential attracting contestants and contestant interaction potentials encoding contest behavior.
Resource potentials can be radially symmetric or anisotropic depending on the biological context.
Contestant interaction potentials feature long-range repulsion, medium-range attraction, and short-range strong repulsion.
Parameters α and δ in the interaction potential represent motivation to escalate and intimidation by the rival, respectively.
The model accounts for different rival assessment strategies influencing interaction parameters.
Nonreciprocal interactions lead to emergent chased dynamics in contests between unmatched rivals.
Adaptive gravity-like attraction explains the mass and velocity profiles of midge swarms.
Adaptivity in interactions arises from sensory systems responding to relative fold-changes in signals.
Behavioral noise is modeled as stochastic terms allowing exploration of potential landscapes.
The contest onset distance defines when contestants switch attention from resource to rival interactions.
The model can simulate fast engage-and-disengage dynamics typical in animal contests.
Effective sizes or resource holding potentials influence the strength and asymmetry of interactions.
The framework can be generalized to many contestants and multiple resources.
The models bridge biological observations with physics-inspired active particle theory.
The paper uses Lambert W functions to describe extrema of interaction potentials.
The contest model has been applied to male spider contests on orb webs.
The adaptive gravity model introduces non-equilibrium properties by violating conservation laws.
